## Source Extractor

Research question: "Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules."

Fetch and extract key claims from this source:
**URL:** https://www.nngroup.com/articles/animation-duration/
**Title:** Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics — Nielsen Norman Group
**Found via:** web-native motion implementation: transitions, scrollytelling, timing numbers search

## Task
1. Use WebFetch to retrieve the page content.
2. Assess source quality: primary research/institution? secondary reporting? blog/opinion? forum? unreliable?
3. Extract 2-5 FALSIFIABLE claims that bear on the research question. Each claim must:
   - be a concrete, checkable statement (not vague generalities)
   - include a direct quote from the source as support
   - be rated central/supporting/tangential to the research question
4. Note publish date if available.

If the fetch fails or the page is irrelevant/paywalled, return claims: [] and sourceQuality: "unreliable".

Structured output only.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

- _gstack-command: Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- academic-paper-composer: Systematic writing framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers from optimized outline to submission-ready manuscript. Use when users want to: (1) write a paper from a detailed outline, (2) ensure quality control during writing, (3) maintain consistency across chapters, (4) prepare a submission-ready manuscript, or (5) systematically execute a planned paper. Triggered by phrases like 'write the paper from this outline,' 'compose the full manuscript,' 'execute the outline,' or when users have completed strategic planning (academic-paper-strategist skill) and are ready to write. Takes optimized outline as input; outputs complete manuscript with iterative quality checks.
- academic-paper-strategist: Systematic strategic planning framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers targeting preprint platforms (PhilArchive, arXiv, PhilSci-Archive). Use when users want to: (1) plan a paper on a specific topic, (2) identify research gaps and assess originality, (3) develop optimized paper outlines, (4) prepare for preprint submission, or (5) understand platform requirements and writing standards. Triggered by phrases like 'plan a paper on,' 'help me design a paper about,' 'identify research gaps in,' 'is this idea original,' or when users need structured research planning. The skill guides through three phases: Platform Analysis (identifying target venue and studying sample papers), Theoretical Framework (AI-driven literature search and gap identification), and Outline Optimization (structured design with reviewer-perspective self-assessment). Each phase includes quality evaluation standards and validation checkpoints. Output: optimized detailed outline ready for systematic writing (use with academic-paper-composer skill).
- apify-ultimate-scraper: Universal AI-powered web scraper for any platform. Use for lead generation, brand monitoring, competitor analysis, influencer discovery, trend research, content analytics, audience analysis, review analysis, SEO intelligence, recruitment, or any data extraction task.

- image-to-code: Elite website image-to-code skill for Codex. For visually important web tasks, it must first generate the design image(s) itself, deeply analyze them, then implement the website to match them as closely as possible. By default, screens should be shown inside a subtle premium iPhone or similar phone mockup with a visible frame, while the main focus stays on the app content itself. This skill generates images only. It does not write code.
- imagegen-frontend-web: Elite frontend image-direction skill for generating premium, conversion-aware website design references. CRITICAL OUTPUT RULE — generate ONE separate horizontal image FOR EVERY section. A landing page with 8 sections produces 8 images. Never compress multiple sections into one image. input.prompt: Extract the full article content including: all specific duration numbers and ranges recommended for UI animations, the thresholds cited (e.g. 0.1s, 1s, 10s response-time limits), easing/motion characteristic recommendations (ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, linear), guidance on distance/size affecting duration, any citations to research, the author name and publish date. Quote exact sentences containing numbers.

content.content:
# UX Animation Duration and Motion Characteristics - Key Findings

**Article Details**
- Author: Page Laubheimer
- Published: February 9, 2020

## Animation Duration Recommendations

**General Range:**
"In general, the duration of most animations should be in the range of 100–500 ms, depending on complexity and on how far the element is traveling."

**Simple Feedback Animations:**
"Simple feedback animations, such as showing a checkbox or toggle switch, should be roughly 100 ms (0.10 seconds) in total duration."

**Substantial Screen Changes:**
"When animation involves substantial screen changes, such as when a modal window moves into view, a duration of 200–300 ms can be appropriate."

**Upper Threshold:**
"At 500ms, animations start to feel like a real drag for users — they become cumbersome and annoying."

**Practical Range:**
"In most cases, a range of 100–400 ms is appropriate, with 400ms being a very slow animation, to be used only for big movements across large screens."

**Disappearance vs. Appearance:**
Objects entering screen typically need longer duration than exiting; "a popup window may take 300ms to appear, but only 200 or 250ms to disappear."

## Easing/Motion Characteristics

**Avoiding Linear Motion:**
"Completely linear motion looks weird and unnatural to users."

**Primary Easing Recommendation:**
"Most frequently, you'll want to use an ease-out animation, that starts quickly but slows down."

**Easing Types Explained:**
The article describes ease-in (slow start, speed up), ease-out (fast start, slow end), and ease-in-out (fastest in middle).

## Distance and Duration Relationship

"The further an element has to move, the more important it is that it does so smoothly and non-jarringly."

## Key Design Principle

"Details matter for UX quality. In animation, this saying is even more accurate than for other design elements."

input.prompt: Does the article mention: prefers-reduced-motion, accessibility, vestibular disorders, the 0.1 second / 1 second / 10 second response-time limits, or cite any research studies/experiments? Quote exact sentences if so. Also quote any statements about spring physics, choreography/staggering, or looping animations.

content.content:
# Content Analysis: Animation Article

**Accessibility & Motion Sensitivity:**
- The article explicitly mentions "prefers-reduced-motion": "you should respect those users who have set their browser or device to 'reduce motion' by removing animations."
- Vestibular disorders are cited: "Parallax, carousel-forwarding animations, and scroll jacking can make users with vestibular disorders dizzy or nauseated and trigger migraines."

**Response Time References:**
- The article references the 0.1 second threshold: "100 ms is at the lower end of perceivable motion" and notes that "100 ms feels **immediate** to users" with a link to "response-times-3-important-limits."

**Research Citations:**
One peer-reviewed study is cited:
- "Pratt, J., Radulescu, P., Guo, R.M., & Abrams, R.A. (2010). It's Alive! Animate motion captures visual attention. Psychological Science, 21, 1724–1730"

**Physics, Choreography, Looping:**
- The article discusses natural motion principles but does NOT mention spring physics specifically, choreography/staggering of multiple elements, or looping animations.

claims.claim: NN/g's baseline duration range for UI animation is 100–500 ms, scaled to complexity and travel distance, with 500 ms as the point where animation starts to feel obstructive; the practical working band is 100–400 ms, and 400 ms is reserved for large movements on large screens. These are stated as craft heuristics in the article, not as results of a measured experiment — the only number with a research lineage is the ~100 ms perceptibility/immediacy floor, which links out to Nielsen's response-time limits.
claims.quote: In general, the duration of most animations should be in the range of 100–500 ms, depending on complexity and on how far the element is traveling. … At 500ms, animations start to feel like a real drag for users — they become cumbersome and annoying. … In most cases, a range of 100–400 ms is appropriate, with 400ms being a very slow animation, to be used only for big movements across large screens.

claims.claim: Duration should be tiered by the size of the state change: micro-interaction feedback (checkbox, toggle) at roughly 100 ms, and substantial screen changes such as a modal entering the viewport at 200–300 ms. This gives a directly usable two-tier number set for micro-interaction versus drawer/sheet/modal motion.
claims.quote: Simple feedback animations, such as showing a checkbox or toggle switch, should be roughly 100 ms (0.10 seconds) in total duration. … When animation involves substantial screen changes, such as when a modal window moves into view, a duration of 200–300 ms can be appropriate.

claims.claim: Exit animations should be shorter than entrance animations for the same element — a popup taking 300 ms to appear should take only 200–250 ms to dismiss. This asymmetry is a concrete, checkable rule for drawer/sheet/modal open-versus-close timing.
claims.quote: a popup window may take 300ms to appear, but only 200 or 250ms to disappear

claims.claim: Linear timing functions are wrong for UI motion; ease-out (fast start, decelerating finish) is the default recommendation for most UI animation. This is a CSS-native, zero-byte technique (`transition-timing-function`) — no runtime required — and directly contradicts a `linear` default.
claims.quote: Completely linear motion looks weird and unnatural to users. … Most frequently, you'll want to use an ease-out animation, that starts quickly but slows down.

claims.claim: NN/g's stated reduced-motion remedy is to REMOVE animation for users who set the reduce-motion preference, and it names parallax, carousel auto-advance and scroll-jacking as triggers for dizziness, nausea and migraine in users with vestibular disorders. This CONFLICTS with the pipeline's rule that every technique must ship a designed reduced-motion still rather than `animation: none` — NN/g is the authoritative source behind the removal convention the pipeline is deliberately overriding, so the repo rule needs to be stated as a deliberate, documented departure rather than an unexamined preference.
claims.quote: you should respect those users who have set their browser or device to 'reduce motion' by removing animations. … Parallax, carousel-forwarding animations, and scroll jacking can make users with vestibular disorders dizzy or nauseated and trigger migraines.
